Decision-Making Capacity and Informed Consent

the four abilities · what consent covers · WIPE exceptions · who decidesCan this patient make this decision now?

Bottom line
  • Capacity is judged by the treating physician for the proposed treatment: the patient communicates a choice, appreciates the consequences, reasons and demonstrates understanding (CARD); competence is a legal finding by a judge
  • Consent is sought from every patient: an involuntary hold, a psychiatric diagnosis or mild intellectual disability does not by itself remove capacity; if drugs or sedation may be interfering and the procedure is not urgent, do not proceed: reassess when the effects wear off
  • Without capacity: the advance directive, then the health care proxy, then family, typically the spouse, adult children, parents, siblings, though the order varies by state; with no one, the best interest standard; a life-threatening emergency is treated without consent

Informed consent needs a patient with capacity, disclosure of the diagnosis and of the benefits, risks and alternatives (including no treatment), and a voluntary choice free from coercion; a patient with capacity may refuse

Decision-making capacity (CARD)
AbilityThe patient shows
Communicates a choiceMakes the decision known
AppreciatesHow the facts and consequences apply to their own situation
ReasonsDescribes how the choice was reached; it need not be the choice the physician prefers
Demonstrates understandingThe benefits, risks and alternatives, including no treatment
Exceptions to informed consent (WIPE)
ExceptionWhen it applies
WaiverThe patient explicitly declines the discussion, as for surgery or research; a patient may also choose not to know
IncompetentUnder 18, or an adult who cannot make the decision: a surrogate decides for the adult; for minors, see
Therapeutic privilegeWithholding information that may harm the patient; only when the harm is very likely, not merely hypothetical
EmergencyA life-threatening condition, when waiting for a surrogate would raise the risk of death or serious harm
Who decides when the patient cannot
Decision makerWhen it decides
Advance directive (living will)First, when it applies to the situation
Health care proxy (durable power of attorney)Next; overrules all family members
Family surrogateWith no proxy: spouse, then adult children, parents, siblings, deciding as the patient would (substituted judgment); the order varies by state
Someone who knows the patient's wishesNo family available
Physicians, by best interestNo living will or surrogate: two-physician consent, or a court-appointed fiduciary
When capacity is in doubt
StepDo
Before judgingRemove communication barriers first
Reversible causesLook for delirium, drug or medication effects, hypoxia, infection or a metabolic derangement; reassess when treated or worn off
InterviewTest the four abilities for this decision; cognitive testing helps but is not required
Still uncertainConsult another clinician or a psychiatrist; the treating physician decides; if doubt remains after a full evaluation, do not restrict the patient's choice, since restricting autonomy needs a high burden of proof
AfterwardRecord the evaluation in the medical record
Commonly confused
PairDecides it
Capacity or competenceCapacity is a medical judgment by the treating physician about a proposed treatment; competence is a legal finding by a judge
Refusal or incapacityRefusing a clearly beneficial treatment may prompt an evaluation, but the patient needs only to reason through the information
Involuntary hold or incapacityA hold does not remove the right to refuse treatment that is not life-threatening
Sedated or incapacitatedDrug effects may be temporary: for a nonurgent procedure, do not proceed; reassess later
Psychiatric illness or incapacityA diagnosis does not remove capacity; poor reasoning from active psychiatric illness can
Surrogate or patientFamily consents only after the patient is found to lack capacity
Family request or disclosureA family asking to withhold a serious diagnosis is usually met by a thoughtful talk with them and sensitive disclosure; withholding (therapeutic privilege) is rare

Pause point. Ask whether this patient can make this decision now: outside a life-threatening emergency, a choice you disagree with, a hold or a diagnosis is no reason to override, and impairment that may wear off means wait and reassess.

Practice
  1. 45-year-old man brought in after a bar fight smells of alcohol and slurs his words A 2-cm scalp cut has stopped bleeding; he refuses stitches and asks to sleep it off Vital signs are normal → Defer the repair and reassess when he is sober → A nonbleeding laceration poses no imminent harm, and alcohol may only temporarily affect his ability to consent, so the repair waits and he is reassessed; a surrogate decides only if he lacks capacity
  2. 70-year-old woman hospitalized with pneumonia wants to go home on day 2 She explains the risks of leaving, including death, and says she accepts them She is alert and oriented; her son demands that she stay → Discharge her against medical advice → She communicates a choice and shows understanding, appreciation and reasoning, so she has capacity and may leave against medical advice; family decides only when capacity is lacking
  3. 78-year-old man is intubated after a stroke and cannot communicate He has no advance directive or health care proxy His wife wants a feeding tube; his adult daughter says he would refuse one → Follow his wife's decision → Without an advance directive or proxy, family members typically decide in the order spouse, adult children, parents, siblings, judging what he would want; two-physician consent is for patients with no surrogate
  4. 82-year-old woman with advanced dementia needs a decision about surgery for a hip fracture Years ago she named her close friend as her health care proxy Her three children disagree with the friend's choice → Follow the health care proxy → A health care proxy holds durable power of attorney and overrules all family members; a court-appointed health fiduciary is an option for patients with no relative or proxy
  5. 30-year-old man arrives unconscious after a car crash with a ruptured spleen and falling blood pressure No family can be reached, and he carries no advance directive The surgeon is ready to operate → Operate without consent → When delay to find a surrogate would raise the risk of death or serious harm, emergency care proceeds without formal consent, on the assumption that a reasonable person would agree
  6. 33-year-old woman with schizophrenia is on an involuntary psychiatric hold She declines removal of a benign-appearing skin mole, citing the scar She is calm, explains the risks and benefits, and repeats her choice → Respect her refusal → Patients on an involuntary hold keep the right to refuse treatment that is not life-threatening, and a psychiatric diagnosis does not by itself remove capacity
Pairs with Adolescent Confidentiality: consent by and for minors. Delirium: a reversible cause of lost capacity.
Transferable rule

Ask whether this patient can make this decision now; without an emergency, a capable refusal stands, and impairment that may wear off means wait and reassess.
